A 48-year-old man with a 12-year history of perianal fistula presented with recent mucinous discharge, pain, and perianal induration. One year earlier, he had undergone incision and drainage of a recurrent perianal abscess. 

On examination, there were two indurated, ulcerative lesions each 7 cm in diameter and three external fistula openings around the anus; there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Upper endoscopy was unremarkable. Colonoscopy showed the internal fistula opening at the right side of the dentate line, with otherwise normal mucosa in the rectum and colon on digital and endoscopic examination.

Abdominopelvic CT and MRI demonstrated a well-defined mass at the level of the anorectal junction extending into the right ischiorectal fossa, with enlarged pelvic lymph nodes but no inguinal nodal or distant metastases.

Histological examination of a biopsy specimen from the indurated area revealed mucinous adenocarcinoma. A serum carcinoembryonic antigen level was within the normal range.

A 31-year-old woman presents with a 4-year history of recurrent painful ulcerations on both legs and feet. She has no personal or family history of vascular or autoimmune disease, denies arthralgia or other dermatologic symptoms, and takes no medications. She also denies tobacco or illicit drug use. On examination, a reticular purplish livedo pattern is noted over both lower limbs. Multiple chronic, nonhealing ulcers are present over the lateral malleolus and the dorsum of the left foot, along with white atrophic scars on the lower legs and ankles. Preliminary diagnostic considerations included thrombophilia, hematologic malignancies, immune-mediated vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, arterial disease, vascular proliferations, diabetes, and medication-induced ulcers. A lesional skin biopsy was performed.

A 10-month-old male infant was brought by his parents for an asymptomatic swelling of the palate.  The mother first noticed the lesion several weeks earlier; no swelling was noted at birth, and the patient’s age limited reporting of pain or tenderness.  On examination, there was a firm, nonmobile mass in the right posterior hard palate extending from the maxillary tuberosity medially almost to the midline.  Multi-detector CT of the maxilla demonstrated a well-defined, expansile lesion of the maxillary crest with mixed radiolucent and radiopaque internal structure, causing thinning and perforation of the maxillary sinus walls and lateral displacement of the nasal cavity wall.  Based on these radiographic findings, a cemento-ossifying fibroma was considered the most likely diagnosis.

A 42-year-old Caucasian man with a 12-year history of well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load, CD4+ count 1184 × 10^6 cell/liter). Past medical history includes treatment for early latent syphilis six years prior. The patient presented with low-grade fever (37.5°) and sudden appearance of skin lesions at the base of his penis. He reported recent sexual activity with multiple male partners. Two days after the initial skin manifestations, he developed fever up to 39°C, chest pain without irradiation, and shortness of breath.

Initial examination revealed vesicular and umbilicated lesions on genitals and small lymphadenomegaly in the groin area. No oropharyngeal lesions were detected. Upon admission for chest symptoms, the patient was hemodynamically stable with continuous anterior chest pain exacerbated by deep breathing.

- Laboratory Tests:    * High-sensitivity cardiac troponin: 128.00 pg/ml initially, peaked at 142.00 pg/ml (reference value < 14 pg/ml)    * Multiple viral serologies including CMV, EBV, Coxsackievirus, Echovirus, Parvovirus B19, and Herpes virus 1/2 were negative (except for past CMV and EBV exposure)    - Imaging Studies:    * ECG: Showed sinus tachycardia with elevated PR segment in aVR lead and depressed in peripheral and thoracic leads    * Echocardiography: Left ventricle diastolic diameter of 59 mm, hypokinetic left ventricle with EF 50%    * Chest CT angiography: Normal, no pulmonary embolism or pneumonia    * Cardiac MRI: Showed slightly increased global T1 and T2 mapping values, minimal hyperintensity of pericardium without effusion, normal biventricular function (EF 57%)    * Coronary CT angiography: Normal    - Continuous Monitoring:    * ECG monitoring showed persistent episodes of sinus pauses (longest 10.1 seconds)    * Episodes of advanced AV block grade 2 Mobitz type 1 and 2    * Sinus bradycardia (heart rate 40-45, nadir 32 pulses/minute while sleeping)

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 28-year-old G2P1 woman presented 31 days after an elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia with worsening headache and easy fatigability for 3 days. The headache was continuous, global, and had become severe over 24 hours, associated with nausea and malaise. Eight days postoperatively she had developed a mild global headache managed with rest and paracetamol. By day 31 the headache was severe, nonpositional, and unrelieved by rest or analgesics. Vital signs were normal. She was fully conscious and oriented, all meningeal signs were negative, and motor function was intact. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, prothrombin time, partial prothrombin time, and international normalized ratio. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a layered hypodense crescent-shaped extra-axial collection over the left frontoparietal convexity with areas of linear and crescentic hyperdensity, measuring 15 mm in width with a 13-mm midline shift.
